description:
The ADR-004 machinery beyond the per-endpoint discipline (which every epic carries as a quality gate): TTL tier registry per endpoint class, in-memory hot-event structures (availability counters, event snapshots) with write-path invalidation, hot-event designation (manual + automatic), cache kill-switch for incidents, staleness tests, and an on-sale read load test proving database reads stay flat while buyer traffic scales.

**Conditions of Success:**
- On-sale load test at the festival-scale NFR (~50-100k capacity, 100k+ queued buyers): buyer-facing read RPS scales while database read load stays near-flat for hot events
- A stale 'sold out'/'available' display decays within its declared tier TTL; correctness always restored at claim time (ADR-002)
- Kill-switch bypasses caches per service without redeploy; staleness/invalidation covered by automated tests
- Storefront call budget audited: one aggregated call per page view, client refresh cadence driven by response TTLs

Lineage: docs/product/brief.md · docs/product/prd-v1.md (capability map) · docs/adr/ADR-004-cache-first-read-path.md

comments.body: COS defined at epic level. Not yet decomposed — US-stories are created when the owner prioritizes this epic (Gate 1). Note: the per-endpoint TTL discipline itself is NOT deferred to this epic — it is a quality gate on every read-endpoint story from US-002 onward (ADR-004).
Backlog grilling 2026-07-12 (owner decisions): load-test COS quantified at festival scale.

### Implementation readiness - CONCERNS

Decomposed 2026-08-04 into five vertical slices, TKT-204..TKT-208. Each is end-to-end for what it claims and demoable on its own; none is a horizontal layer.

| Criterion | Status | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Quality gates extracted | OK | `make check` on every child; browser evidence on TKT-208 only, which is the only child that can change rendered output |
| Vertical slices, one reviewable PR each | OK | C1 is a prefactor (mechanical), C2/C3 one service each, C4 the harness, C5 the storefront |
| Prefactoring split out first | OK | TKT-204 is the prefactor: the tier registry exists so C2/C3's cache lifetime and the response header cannot disagree |
| Ordered by dependency, no forward dependency | OK | 204 -> 205 -> {206, 207}; 208 independent |
| AC verifiable everywhere | OK | Every COS is a counter, a state, or a written artifact. No "works correctly" |
| Links + cycle check | OK | Three `blocked-by` edges, a tree, no cycle |
| Context-memo baked per child | OK | All five, `capturedAt` 2026-08-04, `governingAdrs` re-resolved against `docs/adr/` today rather than copied from the epic |
| No unvalidated assumption a child silently depends on | CONCERN | See concerns 1 and 3 |

**Mapping to the epic's four COS** - every one is owned, none is orphaned:

| Epic COS | Owner |
|---|---|
| On-sale load test: read RPS scales, database read load flat | TKT-207 (proves what TKT-205/206 ship) |
| Stale sold-out/available decays within its tier; correctness restored at claim time | TKT-205, TKT-206 |
| Kill-switch bypasses caches per service without redeploy; staleness/invalidation tested | TKT-205 (builds it), TKT-206 (extends it) |
| Storefront call budget audited; refresh cadence driven by response TTLs | TKT-208 |

**Concerns:**

1. **Hot-event *designation* is carved out of the epic, deliberately** (affects TKT-205). The epic's description names "hot-event designation (manual + automatic)"; **no epic COS requires it**, and population-by-access delivers the same operational result without an operator surface to build, document and get wrong. Recorded as a decision on TKT-205 rather than silently dropped. If TKT-207's load proof shows access-driven population insufficient, that is a follow-up ticket with evidence behind it.

2. **Two caching layers will stack on catalog's event reads** (affects TKT-206). The storefront's SSR `PageDataCache` already fronts exactly those three reads (ADR-004 amendment TKT-128). A second layer with an independent TTL adds its staleness to the first unless invalidation is authoritative end-to-end. TKT-206's plan is required to state the total worst-case staleness, not just catalog's own.

3. **TKT-208 carries one open `uncertainties` item with `owner: human`** - whether the festival page's HTML should become cacheable is a product staleness judgement, not a technical one. Under this run's owner-waived gates the agent decides it and writes the reason into ADR-004. Flagged so the decision is visible in the thread rather than absorbed into an implementation.

4. **TKT-207 touches the gate's smoke suite**, which already has a live flake (TKT-149: a single 5xx in 250 requests fails `TestOnsaleLoadProof`). A read stage that is more flake-prone than the write stage would tax every future ticket. Called out as a review focus, not a blocker.

**Verdict: CONCERNS** - proceedable. The structure holds and every epic COS has an owner; the four concerns are named risks the owner can take eyes-open, and three of the four are already written into the affected child's own readiness comment.

---

**Gate 1 waived by the repo owner** for this run (process experiment, fully autonomous Ready-to-Done). The epic and all five children were moved `Backlog -> Ready` by the agent on the owner's standing instruction rather than by a human drag. Recorded here so the board history shows this epic was never human-prioritized child by child.

```yaml
stage: done
epic: TKT-31 — Read-path caching & hot-event serving
children: TKT-204, TKT-205, TKT-206, TKT-210 (split out mid-run), TKT-207, TKT-208 — all Done and merged
gates: ALL FOUR WAIVED across every child (owner-directed process experiment)
```

### The four epic COS, each with its evidence

| COS | Owner | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| On-sale load test: read RPS scales while database read load stays flat | **TKT-207** | Measured, not asserted: 5× the offered rate (24 → 120 requests) moved the database **not at all**; with caches off the same endpoints took **60 and 30** queries — one per request per statement |
| A stale display decays within its declared tier; correctness restored at claim time | **TKT-205, TKT-206** | TTL from `cachetier`, never a literal. Write-path invalidation at the store commit. `Age` headers stop catalog's tier and the storefront's stacking into ~600s. The claim path is structurally barred from the cache |
| Kill-switch bypasses caches per service without redeploy; staleness and invalidation tested | **TKT-210** | `GET`/`PUT /internal/cache-control` on both services, toggling live processes in the smoke suite |
| Storefront call budget audited; refresh cadence driven by response TTLs | **TKT-208** | One aggregated call per page view, asserted against **real rendered pages**; poll cadence derived from each response |

**ADR-004 rule 2 — accepted and unimplemented since 2026-07-12 — is now implemented, on two services, and proven.**

### What shipped

**Six PRs**, ~**6,900 lines**, three new ADRs (044, 045, and ADR-004's festival amendment), zero rollbacks, `make check` green on `main` after every merge.

### Decomposition — how it held up

Five slices, ordered by dependency. Two things changed mid-run and both were the right call:

1. **TKT-205 was split** at plan-final: the kill-switch became **TKT-210** because a ticket cannot pass Gate 4 half-merged.
2. **TKT-207 was resequenced behind TKT-210**, because its control arm — the half that makes it evidence rather than decoration — needs a way to turn the caches off, and inventing a second one would have left two switches for one state.

Neither was foreseeable at decomposition; both were caught by a plan draft reading the real code.

### overrides — the consolidated list an owner should read

Every review pass across every child returned `needs-attention`. **All 24 findings were fixed.** Four decisions departed from a recommendation, and five commits shipped unreviewed by a second model:

| # | Ticket | Departure |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 204 | Declined an opaque `Tier` + Must/error split — more API than the risk removed |
| 2 | 205 | Kept 500 (not 503) for a too-slow read; **not a regression**, and 503 needs a contract change → **TKT-211** |
| 3 | 206 | Fixed monotonicity with a high-water mark rather than a monotonic clock; residual predates the ticket → **TKT-212** |
| 4 | 208 | Rejected an `s-maxage` parsing claim **with evidence** — the directive has no hyphen, so the regex cannot match it |
| 5 | 210 | **Merged with `hermetic-smoke` red** — proven pre-existing by running it on `main` → **TKT-213** |

Unreviewed final commits: `4304c660`, `9cc81a7c`, `e5cdd6fa`, `9c51dd41`/`2656fa21`, `19f544ed`, `4feeee23`. Each is named in its ticket's ai-review comment, its PR review-guide, and its commit message.

**Five follow-ups carved out rather than smuggled in:** TKT-209, 211, 212, 213, plus TKT-141 left explicitly untouched.

### learnings

**One finding dominates this epic, and it recurred five times.**

> **A test's name is a claim. Check that its assertions pin that claim.**

- **TKT-204**: the spec audit could pass while auditing nothing — deleting every declaration left it green.
- **TKT-205**: the in-flight ceiling test *waited for ten concurrent loads*, then asserted the bookkeeping map held three. It demonstrated the ceiling was broken and passed.
- **TKT-206**: "age is monotonic under a backward clock" pinned only the upstream-age floor; a live entry could still shrink 50 seconds of freshness.
- **TKT-210**: three mutations came back green, one revealing a branch I had just added was inert.
- **TKT-208**: the call-budget test measured the api.ts wrappers, not the pages — and the cadence test would have served `max-age=5` against a former `POLL_MS = 5000`, unable to tell derivation from coincidence.

The common repair each time: ask **what quantity the guarantee actually ranges over** before writing the assertion. Concurrent *queries*, not map size. Peak *concurrency*, not bookkeeping. The *page*, not the wrapper.

The related pattern, four times over: **prose contradicting code**. `statementsPerLoad: 1` beside a comment saying two. A doc comment asserting every call site was a package initializer while one was on a request path. A smoke helper claiming it restored both services when `t.Fatalf` made that impossible. A plan-final forbidding a wrapper test, followed by a wrapper test.

**Promotable to `docs/learnings/` (9 items, each with its ticket):** assert-the-invariant-not-the-bookkeeping · a-cached-test-result-is-a-gate-that-did-not-run · guard-insertion-and-you-have-guarded-half · a-commit-seam-only-catches-what-commits · an-operationId-is-not-a-key · a-test-in-smoke-is-a-test-behind-docker · a-measurement-ticket's-defects-are-silent · writing-the-warning-is-not-heeding-it · two-caching-layers-stack-unless-invalidation-is-authoritative.

### retro

**(1) What would have made this epic faster or better?**

- **The cross-model plan draft earned its keep every single time.** It found `commitAvailability` (TKT-205's whole design), that `PublishPerformance` is autocommit (TKT-206's whole design — reusing TKT-205's seam would have silently missed publishing), that `pg_stat_statements` was already wired (TKT-207), and it corrected **three factual errors in my briefs**. My "here's the real code" sections are assertions; the drafter is what checks them.
- **Adversarial review found 24 real defects, including 6 [high].** On TKT-207 — where the deliverable is a measurement — three of five findings would have left the proof *passing* while proving less than claimed. None would have failed a gate.
- **The cost is concentrated and visible:** ai-review was 44–52% of wall-clock on the two largest tickets. That is the price of the two [high] correctness bugs it caught in the availability cache alone.

**(2) What should the humans change?**

- **`docs/learnings/` + `docs/LEARNINGS.md`:** the 9 items above. The first two change how much a green local gate is worth.
- **`AGENTS.md`, local-gate bullet:** record that `make test-go` runs `-count=1` because a cached pass hid a real failure for four runs (TKT-210), so nobody optimises it back.
- **`.claude/skills/sdlc-ticket/SKILL.md`, three edits**, each earned by a repeat: (a) **a mutation that fails to compile is not a red** — logged on five tickets and still unapplied; (b) the ai-review prompt for a measurement ticket should ask *"what would this still report if the thing it measures were absent?"*; (c) when implementation cannot achieve what plan-final specified, that is an **amendment with a stated reason**, posted before the code ships — not a silent substitution.
- **`hermetic-smoke` has been red on `main` with nobody noticing** (TKT-213). A weekly workflow whose failures reach no one reports nothing.

**On the experiment itself.** Zero human-wait across six tickets; total agent time ~5h. The machinery caught the ordinary defects — every gate failure was real, every review pass found something. What it could not do is settle whether the five overrides above were the right calls; that is what the `overrides:` list exists for, and it is the smallest thing an owner needs to read to re-take those decisions. **A fixed finding and an overridden one look identical in a merged diff**, which is exactly why they are enumerated rather than summarised.
